text: Here's the scenario for this lab. The moment a Priority 1 incident is created, two things should happen automatically: post an alert to a Teams channel so the on-call team sees it right away, and look up extra account information from an external CRM's REST API, so the incident carries the customer's account tier without anyone checking a second system by hand. The trigger itself — Incident created, Priority is 1 Critical — is nothing new from earlier chapters.

Because Microsoft Teams has a pre-built spoke, the first half needs no REST configuration at all. Drop in the Teams Spoke's Post Message action, pick the on-call team's channel from the spoke's own configuration fields, and build a message template from data pills carried forward from the trigger — something like: P1 incident, the incident number, created, then the short description. No endpoint, no headers, no auth profile to configure — the spoke already knows how to reach Teams and authenticate against it.

The CRM has no spoke, so the second half uses the generic REST step. Method is GET, since this is a lookup, not a change to the CRM's data. The endpoint is built from a Connection and Credential Alias pointing at the CRM's API base URL, rather than a URL and credential typed directly into this one flow. Headers carry whatever the CRM requires, and the incident's account identifier goes along as a data pill carried forward from the trigger, used to look up the right account.

The CRM's JSON response includes an account_tier field. Response mapping turns that field into a new data pill, call it crm_account_tier, that the rest of the flow can use. A final Update Record action then writes that value onto the originating incident, referencing the data pill exactly the way any other action in this course references one — so any agent opening the ticket sees the account tier without opening the CRM separately.

Laid out top to bottom: trigger, then the Teams Spoke's Post Message action configured with no code, then a generic REST step calling the CRM through an alias and mapping account_tier into a data pill, then an Update Record action writing that pill back onto the incident. Two different integration mechanisms, chosen for two different reasons, with zero custom script steps anywhere in the flow.
Next up: reading the flow execution log, so when something like this doesn't behave as expected, you know exactly where to look.
